# Discussion

In this prospective, multicentre observational study,
`r n_agcs["final"]` CONTRAfluran canisters recaptured
`r round(recovery_pct_final, 1)`% of the sevoflurane attributable to
these canisters in `r n_ors["final"]` ORs in two European countries.

This capture efficiency is lower than the 34%
reported in our previous single-centre study for CONTRAfluran and sevoflurane [@Gibb2025].
However, that estimate pooled data from two operating rooms that differed markedly
(21.4% and 47.8%)
and our multicentre estimate falls within that range.

Other clinical studies reported 25% to 45%
using different endpoints.
Hinterberg et al. used one CONTRAfluran canister per patient
and desorbed 80 unsaturated canisters in a single batch.
They recovered 25% of the administered desflurane [@Hinterberg2022].
Mulier et al. weighed CONTRAfluran canisters before and after each case
during minimal-flow sevoflurane anaesthesia
and estimated 45% *in vivo* mass transfer [@Mulier2024a].
This measure does not distinguish water from sevoflurane
and does not include losses during storage and desorption,
which are reflected in our capture efficiency.

Even under ideal conditions a canister cannot capture all of the administered sevoflurane.
Part of the delivered sevoflurane is taken up by the patient,
exhaled over the following days
and never reaches the canister [@Dunz2026].
Simulations of 6 h of anaesthesia with the GasMan software [@Philip2015]
showed that only 50% of the delivered sevoflurane reached the canister
at a fresh gas flow of 0.3 l.min⁻¹
and 61% at 0.5 l.min⁻¹ [@Gibb2024b].
The median fresh gas flow of our cohort was
`r fmt_num(flow_inhalational[2L])` l.min⁻¹
during inhalational anaesthesia.
Our estimate of `r round(recovery_pct_final, 1)`% lies well below both
theoretical limits.
Possible reasons are breathing system leaks,
desorption from the canister during TIVA and while flushing the breathing circuit
with high fresh gas flows between cases [@Kalmar2024c],
water competing with sevoflurane for adsorption [@Abiko2010]
and loss during storage [@Gibb2025].

Of the `r n_eligible` eligible canisters we selected `r n_agcs["final"]` for the desorption process by
nearest-neighbour clustering to obtain a homogeneous batch and avoid the
selection of extreme cases.
Among the `r fmt_count(n_excl_outlier)` excluded canisters, two
were the only canisters used in the respective ORs
and therefore received all `r n_bottles_per_or` sevoflurane bottles,
yet their weight gain was no higher than that of canisters
exposed to a fraction of that amount,
and the SENSOfluran unit never indicated saturation.
This may be explained by the post hoc observations in these two ORs
as in one OR, a large proportion of procedures used the da Vinci^TM^ robotic
surgical system (Intuitive Surgical Inc., Sunnyvale, CA, USA),
which may have limited sevoflurane exposure due to high gas exchange in the
capnoperitoneum.
In the other OR, extended TIVA phases may have allowed
previously adsorbed sevoflurane to desorb from the activated charcoal
[@Kalmar2024c; @Wenzel2024].
These are two different mechanisms:
sevoflurane administered may never reach the canister and
sevoflurane already adsorbed may leave it again.
Both limit direct comparisons of capture efficiency across ORs.
Retrospective review further revealed that the SENSOfluran indicator unit
in the second of these ORs had not been recalibrated within the manufacturer's
recommended service interval during the study period,
potentially rendering canister exchange timing unreliable.
Automatic bypass systems that disconnect the canister during TIVA phases
could reduce desorption losses and should be evaluated.
Including these canisters would have lowered the reported capture efficiency.

Approximately `r round((1 - zeosys_yield) * 100, 0)`% of the weight gain of our canisters
was water rather than sevoflurane.
An increasing water content progressively reduces the adsorption capacity
of coconut shell activated charcoal for organic solvent vapours [@Abiko2010].
A water trap between the anaesthesia machine and the canister
may therefore improve capture.
In our study, however, its installation was centre-specific.
Its effect can therefore not be separated
from differences in anaesthetic management
or from other unmeasured centre-level factors.
The same applies to the anaesthesia machines,
which were likewise centre-specific.
Investigating the effect of a water trap requires a design
in which its use varies within centres.

Of the `r n_agcs["final"]` canisters,
`r sum(!is.na(final_wdiff))` were weighed twice at ZeoSys before desorption.
During these `r zeosys_storage_days` days they lost
`r round(zeosys_total_wloss_g, 0)` g of weight in total.
This corresponds to almost two thirds of a sevoflurane bottle
if the lost mass was entirely sevoflurane.
The additional desorption during transport and storage
before the first ZeoSys weighing was not quantified.
The first weighing took place
`r zeosys_days_studyend_to_weight1` days after the last study OR finished,
much longer than the `r zeosys_storage_days` days between the two weighings.
The true loss is therefore even higher.
This spontaneous desorption during storage was described in our previous study [@Gibb2025].
It highlights the need for short storage times and fast processing.

A low capture efficiency does not mean that the canisters failed.
Minimal fresh gas flows lower both sevoflurane use and capture efficiency.
Higher flows would raise the capture efficiency but waste sevoflurane [@Gibb2024b].
Reducing fresh gas flows therefore remains most important.
Canisters can then capture the excess sevoflurane
that still leaves the breathing circuit at the exhaust port [@Gibb2024b; @Mulier2024a].

A comprehensive life cycle assessment,
including the desorption and reprocessing of captured sevoflurane,
is needed to evaluate the environmental impact of vapour capture systems in
general.
Looking further ahead, integration into anaesthesia machines could allow
canisters to be automatically bypassed when no volatile anaesthetics are
present in the exhaust gas.

This study has several limitations.
The single desorption batch precludes between-batch comparisons of desorption yield
and limits the primary outcome to a single-point estimate
without an empirical measure of batch-to-batch variability.
The sample size was determined by the minimum batch size
and not by a formal power calculation.

Sevoflurane consumption was derived from the number of bottles issued per OR.
Neither the vaporizer nor the bottles were weighed.
The vaporizer was filled from a non-study bottle before the first case
and that filling was administered without being counted.
The study ended when the vaporizer was filled from the last study bottle.
A comparable mass remained in the vaporizer and was counted but not administered.
The refill volume of the installed Draeger Vapor 2000 and 3000 vaporizers
(Draegerwerk AG & Co. KGaA, Luebeck, Germany) is 260 ml
and close to the 250 ml of a single bottle.
The vaporizer was full at the start
so the mass remaining at the end can never exceed it.
Sevoflurane consumption is therefore never overestimated
and the reported capture efficiency is an upper bound.
In the worst case the vaporizer was emptied
before the last bottle had been completely poured in.
Up to 11 bottles would then have been administered per OR.
The refill strategy was not recorded.
The capture efficiency would fall to `r round(recovery_pct_final * 10 / 11, 1)`%
if this extreme case applied to every OR.

A further source of uncertainty concerns the `r n_excl_lost` canisters
that could not be located at ZeoSys before desorption.
It is unclear whether these were lost during postal transit,
received but not matched to the study inventory,
or misplaced at some other point in the collection chain.
The courier's delivery receipt confirms arrival at ZeoSys
for all canisters from the centre that did not contribute to the analysis.

The study protocol planned an exploratory analysis
of the clinical factors influencing capture efficiency.
ZeoSys set the minimum batch size of 80 canisters
after the protocol had been finalised.
A meaningful statistical analysis was no longer possible
with the resulting sample
and it was therefore not performed.

Since individual saturation levels were not assessed,
the relative contribution of incomplete canister loading
to the reported capture efficiency cannot be quantified.

Finally, participation was voluntary,
and the centres that joined may not represent the wider anaesthesiology community.
Institutions committed to environmental sustainability tend to use minimal-flow anaesthesia
(median `r fmt_num(flow_inhalational[2L])` l.min⁻¹ during inhalational anaesthesia in our cohort),
which is associated with a lower capture efficiency [@Gibb2024b].
The study covered two countries,
but Germany and Austria share similar healthcare systems,
anaesthesia training, and clinical practice.
